sections.h2: How soon can a Mission house be sold?
sections.html: Selling for cash can take just weeks. Investors and buyers acting for out-of-town heirs are active here, and owners often choose cash after inheriting a house, moving away from the Valley or facing repairs. Keep your deed and tax bill handy.

Mission is a Hidalgo County city on the Rio Grande, founded in 1908 when the Missouri Pacific Railroad set up a station near the center of a new development. It takes its name from La Lomita Chapel, and the population is approaching 70,000. The area is where citrus was first planted in the Rio Grande Valley, and the Texas Citrus Fiesta marks that heritage each year.

That history is the backdrop to the local housing stock, which mixes older parcels near the center with newer lots farther out.

sections.h2: Which sale routes does a Mission owner have?
sections.html:
You have three paths, and each runs on its own clock.

  • Cash buyer. A fit for as-is sales, clouded inherited title and storm or roof damage.
  • Agent listing. May bring more for a home in good shape, though showings and loan timelines come with it.
  • Seller financing. Slower and regulated. A contract for deed on a residence is governed by Property Code chapter 5, and the buyer keeps a right to cancel.

Insist on written offers and learn who pays for title, recording and survey.

sections.h2: Old land records and clear title
sections.html:
Land around Mission began as Spanish porciones, long strips running about two-thirds of a mile along the river and 11 to 16 miles inland. Porciones 55 and 57 held Rancho La Lomita, home of the chapel, and a land company later developed the area around the 1908 railroad station.

Because of that start, older Mission parcels may show long ownership chains in county records, and a title search follows every link. Land held by a family for generations calls for gathering old deeds, family agreements and probate papers, since a gap can hold up a sale. Ask a cash buyer's title company early what it needs.

sections.h2: Building permits and repairs in Mission
sections.html:
Mission's Inspections Division reviews permits for new buildings and checks compliance with minimum building codes. A permit is also required for any concrete or asphalt slab with a value of $100 or more, and mobile homes need permits.

Inspectors check foundation, plumbing, framing, mechanical, A/C, electrical, setbacks, sidewalks and buffering on new residences. Structures that existed before annexation are treated as grandfathered while they stay as they are, but expanding one requires a permit and brings zoning and setback rules into play. The division's phone is 956-580-8691. Prior to listing, find out whether any addition, slab or carport was permitted. Open work can hold up a buyer's lender.

sections.h2: Hidalgo appraisal district and tax dates
sections.html:
Hidalgo CAD sets values for Mission property. Homestead and over-65 applications go through its online portal, and you can reach customer service by phone at 956-381-8466.

Homestead notices land around April 1, with protests due by mid-May. State law holds a homestead's appraised value to a 10 percent rise per year. Ask the district which exemptions sit on your account so a buyer knows what happens after closing.

sections.h2: Homestead exemptions for a Mission buyer
sections.html:
A buyer who moves in can apply for the residence homestead exemption. School taxes drop by $140,000 of value, and an owner 65 or older or disabled gets $60,000 more.

  • Even when you never filed, a buyer who closes after January 1 can get it at once for that year.
  • For a disabled veteran the amount is $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, and a full 100 percent rating can exempt the whole homestead.
  • Heirs missing from the deed may still apply, using an ownership affidavit, a death certificate and a utility bill.

sections.h2: What if unpaid taxes lead to a tax sale?
sections.html:
Unpaid taxes are backed by a lien the county can foreclose. It attaches each January 1, and a court may take the property even after a sale. Expect court costs, plus up to 20 percent for contract attorneys.

Getting land back after a tax sale is hard. A homestead owner has two years from the filing of the purchaser's deed, and pays costs plus a 25 percent premium in year one or 50 percent in year two. Other property gets just 180 days. A former owner can claim excess proceeds for two years. Start by asking the tax office for a payoff and itemized statement.

  • Homeowners over 65 or disabled can use installments.
  • Some collectors offer plans running up to 36 months, and a homestead must be offered one.
  • Penalty and interest waivers must be requested in writing.

sections.h2: How a Mission seller compares offers
sections.html:
Reduce each bid to the same terms before you pick. The highest price with a slow inspection period can pay less than a smaller cash bid that closes fast.

  • Dollar amount and as-is status.
  • Closing date and title company.
  • Fees for title, recording and survey, and who pays.
  • Earnest money and its fate if the buyer leaves.
  • Loan or appraisal conditions.

Get final figures on a closing statement, and take questions about confusing lines to the title company.

Your accepted offer triggers a title search. The company reads county records for liens, tax balances and gaps in who owned the land, which matters most with older Mission parcels where a missing heir or an unreleased lien can turn up late. Each problem must be resolved before anyone signs the deed.

Bring the deed, your newest tax bill, a loan payoff letter and permit papers for additions. Closing takes one sitting. You sign, the county clerk records the deed, your loan and taxes are paid from the funds, and the remainder is yours. A buyer with a mortgage adds an appraisal that may reopen the price. Cash buyers generally skip that step.

Proceeds at closing cover any liens and taxes. Inherited property brings a request from the title company for court orders or recorded papers showing who may sign, and probate of a will has a four-year limit from the death.

Foreclosure is usually a nonjudicial auction on a first Tuesday, preceded by 21 days' notice, and a deficiency suit has a two-year window. Selling beforehand leaves the equity in your hands.

sections.h2: Where a Mission deed is recorded
sections.html: Once notarized, the deed is filed with the county clerk where the land sits. The 2023 manual lists $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for every later page, with records fees capped. Ask the clerk what is charged now.

sections.h2: Questions to ask a buyer before signing
sections.html: Before you sign, learn the purchaser's identity, whether the offer is as-is and who holds the earnest money. Ask about the closing date and the plan if title trouble appears. Read every page of the contract, and have the title company, not the buyer, prepare your closing statement.

faqs.q: Is a storm-damaged Mission house sellable?
faqs.a: Yes, to cash buyers who price in the repairs. Listing usually means fixing damage for lender approval.

faqs.q: When does Mission require a permit for concrete?
faqs.a: For any slab worth $100 or more. Expanding an older structure also needs a permit and brings zoning setbacks into play.

faqs.q: Who sets appraised values in Mission?
faqs.a: The Hidalgo County Appraisal District. Reach customer service at 956-381-8466 or use its portal for homestead and over-65 filings.

faqs.q: What proves I can sell an inherited house?
faqs.a: A muniment of title, administration or a transfer on death deed. A will must be probated within four years of death.
If closing happens before the auction, yes. Texas allows 20 days to reinstate after the default notice and at least 21 days' notice of sale.
